title: Phishing vs Spam: The Difference That Matters
hook: Not every unwanted email is phishing. But every phishing email wants something from you.
explanation: Spam is unwanted bulk email. Phishing is a targeted attempt to trick someone into revealing credentials, approving a payment, opening a malicious file, or giving an attacker access.
takeaway: Before you click, pause and check the sender, the request, and the destination link.
visual: A split-screen graphic: harmless spam on the left, a fake Microsoft 365 sign-in email on the right. Add three red flags with arrows.
gif: An inbox message morphs into a fake login page, then a red stop sign appears before the click.

title: MFA Is Important, But It Is Not Magic
hook: MFA protects passwords. It does not automatically protect every session.
explanation: Attackers can use fake sign-in pages, MFA fatigue, or stolen browser sessions to get around weak MFA setups. MFA remains essential, but it works best with phishing-resistant methods and sign-in monitoring.
takeaway: Use an authenticator app or security key, never approve an unexpected prompt, and review unfamiliar sign-ins.
visual: A password gate, an MFA gate, and a separate browser-session path. Show that the third path needs its own protection.
carousel: How attackers try to bypass it
gif: A password lock closes, then a notification storm appears; the user rejects it and the attack path fades out.

title: What a VPN Actually Does
hook: A VPN is not a magic invisibility cloak. It is an encrypted tunnel.
explanation: A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN server, especially useful on untrusted networks. It does not make unsafe downloads safe or stop every website from identifying you.
takeaway: Think of a VPN as one security control in a larger toolkit—not a replacement for good browsing habits.
visual: Laptop to public Wi-Fi to a protected tunnel to VPN server to website; show the exposed and encrypted portions clearly.
gif: Data packets travel openly, enter a coloured tunnel, and emerge safely at the other end.

title: Why Security Patching Cannot Wait Forever
hook: A vulnerability is an unlocked door in software. A patch is the fix before someone uses it.
explanation: Vendors release patches when they fix known weaknesses. Attackers often scan for systems that have not applied publicly available fixes, so patching reduces an already-known risk.
takeaway: Know your critical assets, test important patches quickly, and have a clear emergency-patching process.
visual: A simple timeline: vulnerability found, patch released, attackers begin scanning, organization patches.
gif: A software door labelled 'known flaw' closes as a patch is applied, while a scanning attacker is blocked.

title: Encryption in Plain English
hook: Encryption changes readable information into a form that only the right key can unlock.
explanation: It protects data when it is being sent and when it is stored. The key is the secret that lets an authorized person turn ciphertext back into readable information.
takeaway: Encryption protects data, but poor key management can still expose it.
visual: A message becomes a locked box, crosses the internet, and is opened with the right key at the destination.
carousel: Where you use encryption every day
gif: A readable message scrambles into unreadable characters and unlocks only with a matching key.

title: What a SIEM Does for a Security Team
hook: A SIEM does not stop every attack. It helps analysts see the story hidden across thousands of events.
explanation: A Security Information and Event Management platform collects logs from devices, users, cloud services, and applications. It helps a security team search, correlate, alert, and investigate.
takeaway: Good detection depends on useful data and well-tuned rules—not just buying a SIEM.
visual: Multiple sources—endpoint, firewall, cloud, identity—flow into a central SOC screen, then into one investigation timeline.
carousel: SIEM is a process, not a magic box
gif: Separate log lines flow into one dashboard and join into a highlighted attack timeline.

title: Ransomware Usually Starts Before Encryption
hook: The ransomware note is often the last visible step—not the beginning of the attack.
explanation: Many ransomware incidents begin with stolen credentials, phishing, exposed remote access, or an unpatched system. Attackers then move through the environment before deploying encryption.
takeaway: Focus on preventing the first foothold: secure identities, patch exposed systems, and monitor suspicious movement.
visual: Five-stage attack path: initial access, privilege escalation, lateral movement, data theft, encryption.
carousel: Encryption and how to break the chain
gif: A five-step attacker path appears; blue-team controls block the path at each stage.

title: Zero Trust Does Not Mean Trust Nobody
hook: Zero Trust means: verify every important request, not just the first login.
explanation: Instead of assuming someone is safe because they are inside the network, Zero Trust checks identity, device health, context, and access need before granting access.
takeaway: Start small: strong identity controls, least privilege, and device checks are practical Zero Trust steps.
visual: A user requests access; identity, device, location, and permission checks appear before a resource opens.
gif: A user passes through four lightweight verification gates before accessing a file.

title: Antivirus vs EDR: Why Both Terms Exist
hook: Antivirus looks for known bad things. EDR helps security teams investigate suspicious behaviour.
explanation: Endpoint Detection and Response tools provide visibility into devices and enable detection, investigation, and response. They add context beyond traditional file-based antivirus protection.
takeaway: A security tool is only useful when alerts are reviewed and response actions are tested.
visual: A laptop with two layers: antivirus blocks a known malicious file; EDR traces suspicious behaviour and gives the analyst response options.
